passage:
"Neelam, you can't seriously think the moon landing was staged."
"Gargi, look at the flag. It waves. There's no air up there."
"Hold on." Gargi put down her chai. "Where did you first see that? I'm curious how you got there."
"A long video my cousin sent. It made a lot of sense."
"Okay. Can I tell you just one thing? The flag had a rod sewn along the top so it stayed out. It looked like waving because they twisted the pole."
"Huh." Neelam frowned. "Nobody mentioned the rod."
"I'm not saying your cousin is silly. It's a clever video. Send it to me? I'll watch it properly."
"Fine 🙂 But I'm not promising to change my mind."
"Deal. More chai?"

qa.q: What did Neelam point to as proof that the moon landing was staged?
qa.a: Neelam pointed to the flag, which waves although there is no air up there.

qa.q: Why did Gargi ask where Neelam first saw the claim, instead of just saying it was wrong?
qa.a: Gargi was curious about how Neelam got there and wanted to respect a friend rather than humiliate, since people rarely change when they feel attacked.

qa.q: What could Gargi do if Neelam still isn't convinced later?
qa.a: Stay friendly, share another single fact when it fits, and keep watching the cousin's video together rather than arguing harder.

qa.q: How does Neelam seem to take Gargi's approach?
qa.a: Neelam did not feel attacked. Agreeing to send the video, while saying no promise to change, shows a friend still honest and at ease.

grounding: A friend holds a conspiracy theory; Gargi asks how they came to it, shares one reliable fact and avoids humiliating them.
